nameStory: The clover looper gets its name from its caterpillar's distinctive way of moving, which creates loops as it inches along clover plants. Like other looper moths, the larvae lack middle legs and must arch their bodies into a loop with each step, creating a characteristic humping motion that's unmistakable once you see it.
description: The clover looper moth is a medium-sized brown moth with subtle patterns that help it blend into grasses and low vegetation. With a wingspan of about 1.2 to 1.6 inches, it's roughly the size of a large postage stamp when its wings are spread. These moths have a muted, earthy appearance with soft brown and tan coloring, making them easy to overlook as they rest during the day. They're one of our more common grassland moths, active from spring through late fall.

idTips.label: Wing size and shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized wings spanning 1.2-1.6 inches with a triangular shape when at rest, held horizontally against the body like a small paper airplane

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Soft brown and tan tones throughout, with subtle darker and lighter bands that create a weathered, dried-grass appearance

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: Sits with wings spread flat and horizontal, hugging close to grass stems or low vegetation rather than holding wings vertically

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Fuzzy, moth-like body that appears soft and downy, not smooth and hard like a beetle

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with an erratic, bouncing motion when disturbed from grass, but generally weak fliers that don't go far

habitat: Look for clover looper moths in open grasslands, meadows, fields, and anywhere clover grows abundantly throughout New England. They're especially common in agricultural areas, pastures, and disturbed sites where their host plants thrive. You'll also find them in suburban areas with large lawns, parks, and along grassy roadsides from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in March and April, becoming active on warm days. Look for them resting in grass during the day or attracted to porch lights on mild evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple generations. Moths are most visible from June through August, often disturbed from grass when walking through fields.
seasonality.fall: Active through October and into November during warm spells. Late-season adults are preparing for winter or laying final eggs before frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active during winter months. The species overwinters in the pupal stage, hidden in soil or plant debris.

funFact: Clover looper caterpillars are nature's tiny acrobats - they can actually measure distances by stretching their bodies out like a living ruler, using their head and back end as measuring points to gauge the gap before making their characteristic looping leap to the next leaf.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small brown grassland moths, but the clover looper's horizontal wing position when resting is distinctive - many similar moths hold their wings more vertically or fold them roof-like over their bodies.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'clover' looper, these moths actually feed on many different plants as caterpillars, including various grasses and lupines. The common name focuses on just one of their favorite foods, which can be misleading for new moth watchers expecting to find them only on clover plants.
compareHints: As the only Caenurgina species regularly found in New England, compare the clover looper to other underwing moths in the Erebidae family by its smaller size and consistently brown coloration. Unlike the larger underwing moths that flash bright colors when they fly, clover loopers maintain their subtle earth tones throughout their wings and never show the dramatic color contrasts of their flashier relatives.
